title: In an array where every number appears exactly twice except for one number that appears once, find that single number using constant extra space. Explain why XOR of all elements gives the answer.
shortTitle: Single Number (Find the One Element That Appears Once)

s1_definition.profdef: Single Number is the foundational Bitwise XOR problem. Because XOR of a number with itself is zero and XOR with zero leaves the number unchanged, XOR-ing every element together cancels each pair and leaves only the unpaired number. This runs in O(n) time and O(1) space, beating a hash-set approach on memory.
s1_definition.analogy: At the National Bank of India, every reconciliation entry should appear twice, once as a debit leg and once as a matching credit leg, except for one orphan entry that was posted only once. If we XOR all the entry codes together, every matched pair cancels out and the lone orphan code remains.
s1_definition.oneliner: XOR all numbers together; pairs cancel to zero and the single unpaired number survives.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Single Number is the foundational Bitwise XOR problem. Because XOR of a number with itself is zero and XOR with zero leaves the number unchanged, XOR-ing every element together cancels each pair and leaves only the unpaired number. This runs in O(n) time and O(1) space, beating a hash-set approach on memory.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** At the National Bank of India, every reconciliation entry should appear twice, once as a debit leg and once as a matching credit leg, except for one orphan entry that was posted only once. If we XOR all the entry codes together, every matched pair cancels out and the lone orphan code remains.

**One line to remember:** XOR all numbers together; pairs cancel to zero and the single unpaired number survives.

sections.s2_technical:
XOR has three properties we rely on: a number XOR itself is zero, a number XOR zero is itself, and XOR is commutative and associative so order does not matter. We start a running result at zero and XOR every element into it: `int result = 0; for (int n : nums) result ^= n;`. Because each paired value appears an even number of times, those values XOR to zero, and only the odd-one-out remains in `result`.

This is strictly better than the obvious approaches. Sorting then scanning is O(n log n); a hash set counting occurrences is O(n) time but O(n) space. The XOR method is O(n) time and O(1) space, which is the senior-level answer the interviewer is looking for.

A senior nuance is that XOR works here precisely because every other element is perfectly paired; if elements could appear three times or some other odd count, this simple XOR would not isolate the single number and we would need bit-counting across positions instead. Complexity is O(n) time and O(1) space.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India posts reconciliation entries in matched debit and credit pairs, but a glitch left exactly one entry unmatched, and operations must find that orphan code without allocating a big lookup structure on a memory-constrained batch node. This is exactly how Single Number works.

Problem 2 — Building a hash set of all codes would work but wastes memory on huge batches. This is why we XOR all codes together so matched pairs cancel and the orphan survives, using only one integer of extra space.

The code defines a `ReconService` exposing `findOrphan(codes)` returning the unmatched code. A `Demo` runs it over a batch with one orphan and logs the orphan code.

sections.s5_journey:
Input: codes 7012, 7045, 7012, 7099, 7045.

Step 1: result starts at 0. XOR 7012 gives 7012.

Step 2: XOR 7045 gives 7012 XOR 7045.

Step 3: XOR 7012 cancels the earlier 7012, leaving 7045.

Step 4: XOR 7099 gives 7045 XOR 7099.

Step 5: XOR 7045 cancels the earlier 7045, leaving 7099, the orphan.

```

INFO: Unmatched reconciliation code = 7099
INFO: Orphan code: 7099
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  codes:[7012,7045,7012,7099,7045]
    │  fold with XOR (identity 0)
    ▼
  0 ^7012 ^7045 ^7012 ^7099 ^7045
    │ paired 7012 cancel, paired 7045 cancel
    ▼
  result = 7099  (the single unmatched code)
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Single Number is the foundational Bitwise XOR problem. Every element appears twice except one, and I exploit three properties of XOR: a number XOR-ed with itself is zero, a number XOR-ed with zero is unchanged, and XOR is order-independent. So if I fold every element into a running accumulator with XOR, each perfectly paired value cancels itself to zero, and the only value left standing is the one that appeared once.

This beats the alternatives on the metric interviewers care about. Sorting and scanning is n log n, and a hash set is linear time but linear space. The XOR fold is linear time and constant space, which is the senior answer. I would be clear that this trick depends on every other element being exactly paired; if elements repeated an odd number of times I would instead count set bits across each bit position.

At the National Bank of India I used this when reconciliation entries, which should always come in matched debit and credit pairs, left exactly one orphan after a glitch, and the batch node was memory-constrained. I XOR-ed all the entry codes together so every matched pair cancelled and the orphan code remained, using just a single integer of extra space. Explaining the self-inverse property of XOR and why it gives constant space is what shows an interviewer I understand the bit-level reasoning rather than just the trick.
